cards.front: Effective Java Item 75 — what should an exception's message contain?
cards.back: The values of the parameters that caused the failure
cards.extra: The message is often all an engineer has: a stack trace plus "index 12" is diagnosable, "invalid index" is not.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
int index = 12;
String bad = "invalid index";
String good = "index=" + index + " size=3";
if (index >= 3) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException(good);

cards.front: Effective Java Item 76 — what is failure atomicity?
cards.back: A failed method leaves the object in the state it had before the call
cards.extra: Achieved by validating first, computing before mutating, or working on a copy. Half-applied updates are the worst kind of bug.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
final class Basket {
  private int count;
  void addAll(java.util.List<String> xs) {
    for (String x : xs) if (x == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("null");
    for (String x : xs) count++; }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 77 — what does an empty catch block tell the reader?
cards.back: That the author did not think about the failure — and it hides real errors
cards.extra: If you cannot handle it, let it propagate. If you ignore it deliberately, log it and comment why.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
int n = 0;
try { n = Integer.parseInt("oops"); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { }
System.out.println(n);

cards.front: Effective Java Item 78 — what makes a field safely shared between threads?
cards.back: Synchronization (or volatile) on every read and write of the shared mutable state
cards.extra: Without it, threads may see stale values forever. The book's example is a flag that a compiler happily hoists out of the loop.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
final class Flag {
  private volatile boolean stopped;
  void stop() { stopped = true; }
  boolean stopped() { return stopped; }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 79 — why should you avoid calling alien methods inside a synchronized block?
cards.back: You lose control of how long the lock is held, which invites deadlock and stalls
cards.extra: Do the minimum inside the lock: read the state, release, then call out. The book calls this open calls.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::04 Java Memory Model
cards.example:
final class Box {
  private int n;
  synchronized int snapshot() { return n; }
  void tell(java.util.function.IntConsumer alien) { alien.accept(snapshot()); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 80 — what replaced raw threads in modern Java?
cards.back: Executors and tasks (ExecutorService, Runnable/Callable), with streams and ForkJoin for data parallelism
cards.extra: A Thread is a scheduling primitive; an executor handles pooling, shutdown and error propagation.
cards.example:
java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService pool = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("task"));
pool.shutdown();
int sum = java.util.stream.IntStream.range(0, 10).parallel().sum();

cards.front: Effective Java Item 81 — why prefer java.util.concurrent to wait/notify?
cards.back: It gives you the correct patterns pre-built: BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, ConcurrentHashMap, locks with conditions
cards.extra: Hand-written wait/notify loops are where most concurrency bugs live.
cards.example:
java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue<String> q = new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
try { q.put("task"); String task = q.take(); System.out.println(task); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String,Integer> counts = new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.merge("task", 1, Integer::sum);
java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch latch = new java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch(1);
latch.countDown();

cards.front: Effective Java Item 82 — why must you document thread safety?
cards.back: Callers otherwise guess, and a wrong guess means too little or too much synchronization
cards.extra: State it explicitly: immutable, thread-safe, conditionally thread-safe, or not thread-safe. Synchronization is part of the contract.
cards.example:
final class Counter {
  /** Thread-safe: all methods are synchronized, so callers need no extra locking. */
  private int n;
  synchronized void inc() { n++; }
  synchronized int get() { return n; }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 83 — when is lazy initialization worth it?
cards.back: Only when the value is expensive and may never be used — and then use the holder class idiom for statics
cards.extra: It adds synchronization complexity and a race if done carelessly. The double-checked idiom needs a volatile field to be correct.
cards.example:
class Lazy {
  private Lazy() { }
  static Lazy get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
  private static class Holder { static final Lazy INSTANCE = new Lazy(); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 84 — why must you never rely on the thread scheduler?
cards.back: Its policy is unspecified and varies by platform — correctness would become non-portable
cards.extra: Do not use Thread.yield or priorities for correctness. Write code that is correct regardless of scheduling.
cards.example:
java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch done = new java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch(1);
Thread t = new Thread(() -> done.countDown());
t.setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY);
t.start();
try { done.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 85 — why prefer alternatives to Java serialization?
cards.back: It is a large attack surface and a long-term compatibility burden; JSON or a schema-based format is safer
cards.extra: Serialization bypasses constructors, so an attacker can craft an object that violates every invariant.
cards.example:
String json = "{\"name\":\"Ada\"}";
System.out.println(json);
java.util.Properties p = new java.util.Properties();
p.setProperty("name", "Ada");
System.out.println(p.getProperty("name"));

cards.front: Effective Java Item 86 — what does implementing Serializable cost you?
cards.back: The class's private fields become part of the API, forever, and the constructor is bypassed
cards.extra: It also exposes you to bugs and security holes. The book: do it deliberately, with a documented serial version UID.
cards.example:
final class Point implements java.io.Serializable {
  private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
  private int x;
  Point(int x) { this.x = x; }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 87 — when is the default serialized form a bad choice?
cards.back: When it freezes an internal representation you might want to change
cards.extra: Custom form (writeObject/readObject) decouples the wire format from the fields.
cards.example:
class Id implements java.io.Serializable {
  private transient int id;
  private void writeObject(java.io.ObjectOutputStream o) throws java.io.IOException { o.writeInt(id); }
  private void readObject(java.io.ObjectInputStream i) throws java.io.IOException { id = i.readInt(); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 88 — why must readObject be written defensively?
cards.back: Deserialization bypasses the constructor, so invariants must be re-established by hand
cards.extra: Treat the incoming stream as hostile: validate, defensively copy mutable fields, and check invariants before use.
cards.example:
final class Range implements java.io.Serializable {
  private int value;
  Range(int v) { if (v < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("v=" + v); this.value = v; }
  private void readObject(java.io.ObjectInputStream in) throws java.io.IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    in.defaultReadObject(); if (value < 0) throw new java.io.InvalidObjectException("value=" + value); }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 89 — for instance control across serialization, what should you use?
cards.extra: readResolve only works if you remember it and get it right; a single-element enum is immune.
cards.example:
enum Singleton { INSTANCE; int id() { return 1; } }
class Ex { static void m() { Singleton s = Singleton.INSTANCE; System.out.println(s.id()); } }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 90 — what is the serialization proxy pattern?
cards.back: Serialize a small private proxy object that reconstructs the real one in readResolve
cards.extra: It keeps the wire format separate from the implementation, and gives the deserializer a constructor to run validation through.
cards.example:
class Holder { private final int v; Holder(int v) { this.v = v; } private Object writeReplace() { return new Proxy(v); } }
class Proxy implements java.io.Serializable { private final int v; Proxy(int v) { this.v = v; } private Object readResolve() { return new Holder(v); } }
